meta.title: The Dashboard Nobody Needed
meta.subtitle: A Good Company flagship case
meta.purpose: Teach the Good Company operating pattern through a realistic AI-assisted product decision.

dgt.digital: All evidence, claims, decisions, approvals, artifacts, outcomes, and learning are represented as persistent objects.
dgt.governed: Colleague responsibilities, authority, reviews, and human approvals remain explicit.
dgt.trustworthy: Material claims expose sources, confidence, contradictions, and verification status.

organization.name: Northline
organization.description: A fictional B2B SaaS company that helps service businesses manage customer onboarding and retention.
organization.trigger: An investor demonstration is ten days away.
organization.initial_request: Build a customer health dashboard with red-yellow-green scores, trend charts, filters, and export before Friday.
organization.stated_goal: Show investors that Northline can help customers reduce churn.
organization.actual_job: Identify which accounts need attention now, understand why, and decide what to investigate next.

characters.name: Mira
characters.core_question: What are we actually trying to change?

characters.name: Echo
characters.core_question: What supports that—and what happened next?

characters.name: Rook
characters.protects: The Company from its own confidence

characters.name: Atlas
characters.core_question: What has to be true for this to work reliably?

characters.name: Nexus
characters.core_question: Who needs to be in the room next?

evidence.title: Investor note
evidence.source: Email from lead investor to Avery
evidence.summary: The investor asked Northline to demonstrate how the product helps teams identify retention risk and take timely action. The note did not request a dashboard.
supports: The desired outcome is risk identification and action, not a specific interface.

evidence.title: Customer-success interviews
evidence.source: Six interviews across four customer organizations
evidence.summary: All six CSMs described daily triage across usage data, CRM notes, renewal dates, and support history. Five said they rarely open the existing dashboard. Four asked for an explanation of why an account was flagged.
supports: Explanations may matter more than additional charts.
The existing dashboard is not the primary working surface.
contradicts: More dashboard views will automatically improve adoption.

evidence.title: Product-usage log
evidence.summary: Fourteen percent of active CSMs opened the current health dashboard in a typical week. Fifty-two percent opened alert emails, but many returned to other systems to verify the alert.
supports: Users respond to exceptions more often than dashboards.
contradicts: The dashboard is the primary way CSMs monitor risk.

evidence.title: Support-ticket language
evidence.source: Thirty-one relevant support tickets from the previous quarter
evidence.summary: Recurring phrases included 'Which accounts changed?', 'Why is this customer marked at risk?', and 'What should I look at first?' Seven tickets used the word dashboard.
supports: The desired progress is prioritization and explanation.
Users use decision language more often than interface language.
contradicts: Dashboard is the dominant customer vocabulary.

evidence.title: Health-score audit
evidence.source: Internal review by Echo and Atlas
evidence.summary: The health score used undocumented weights. Renewal dates were missing for eighteen percent of accounts. Missing data was sometimes treated as a negative signal rather than an inability to observe.
supports: The current score should not be presented as an unquestioned fact.
Insufficient data requires a separate system state.
contradicts: Red-yellow-green status is reliable enough to drive action.

evidence.title: Internal product assumption
evidence.source: Planning note repeated in three internal conversations
evidence.summary: The team believed investors expected a dashboard because dashboards are common in SaaS demonstrations. No direct source supported the belief.

claims.text: Customer-success teams need a faster way to identify accounts requiring attention.
A dashboard is the correct product form.
Users need to understand the evidence behind a risk signal.
The existing health score is sufficiently trustworthy to drive action.
Automatic next-action recommendations will improve follow-through.

decision_options.label: Build the full dashboard
decision_options.summary: Implement the original request before the investor demonstration.
decision_options.preview: A polished interface may be completed quickly, but the current evidence does not show that it improves the CSM's decision.

decision_options.label: Research longer
decision_options.summary: Pause implementation until a larger discovery study is complete.
decision_options.risk: Low product risk; high timing cost
decision_options.preview: This reduces premature commitment but misses the opportunity to learn from a bounded pilot before the deadline.

decision_options.label: Reframe as an Attention Queue pilot
decision_options.summary: Build the smallest product that helps eight CSMs identify accounts needing review and inspect the evidence behind each signal.
decision_options.preview: This directly tests the supported job while preserving human judgment and exposing uncertainty.

decision_options.label: Reject the initiative
decision_options.preview: The dashboard request is weak, but the underlying customer problem has credible support.

approved_decision.name: Account Attention Queue pilot
scope: Show accounts that require review rather than every account.
Expose the signal, source, change, confidence, and data freshness.
Separate risk, stable, and insufficient-data states.
Allow a CSM to mark reviewed, investigate, or defer.
Keep any next-action suggestion clearly experimental.
Do not automatically contact a customer or change an account status.
prohibited_assumptions: A risk score is a fact.
Suggested actions may be executed without human review.
success_conditions: A pilot CSM can identify the accounts needing review in under fifteen minutes.
Every flag links to inspectable evidence.
Insufficient data is visible as its own state.
No external action occurs without human authorization.
The pilot captures use, triage time, evidence inspection, overrides, and feedback.

workflows: Create an attention item when a supported exception exists.
Link each item to evidence and confidence.
Route the item to the account owner.
Require a human decision before external action.
technical_acceptance: Missing source data produces 'Insufficient data,' not 'At risk.'
Every attention item includes source, timestamp, and confidence.
No automated customer outreach exists in the pilot.
cognitive_acceptance: A CSM can explain why an account appears.
A CSM can distinguish evidence from recommendation.
The interface does not require remembering information from another screen.
The next valid action is visible.
Uncertainty is communicated without false precision.

predictions.text: The Attention Queue will reduce median daily triage time.
Evidence links will be used when CSMs evaluate a flag.
predictions.expected: Opened for at least half of flagged accounts

predictions.text: Suggested next actions will improve follow-through.
predictions.expected: Accepted for at least half of reviewed accounts

predictions.text: Separating insufficient data will reduce false risk interpretation.
predictions.expected: No missing-data account displayed as confirmed risk

metrics.label: Weekly active use
metrics.interpretation: Strong adoption signal within the small pilot.

metrics.label: Suggested-action acceptance
metrics.interpretation: P-03 weakened; suggestions were often described as generic.

metrics.label: Missing-data errors
metrics.interpretation: P-04 only partially supported; Atlas added stricter observability checks.

qualitative: CSMs described the queue as 'a place to start' rather than another report.
Users valued seeing why an account appeared.
Users preferred choosing the next action themselves.
The pilot revealed that data availability needed to be modeled before risk.
outcome.correction: Atlas added a mandatory observability check and a separate Insufficient data state before any risk state can be assigned.
outcome.canonical_learning: In Northline's eight-person pilot, exception-based triage reduced time-to-priority and produced stronger weekly use than the existing dashboard. Evidence links were frequently inspected. Automatic next-action recommendations did not yet demonstrate value. These findings are limited to the pilot context and should not be generalized to all dashboards or customer-success teams.

dashboard.headline: The dashboard shipped. The decision did not improve.
details: Two of eight pilot CSMs opened the dashboard during the following month.
The team still relied on spreadsheets and CRM notes for triage.
Six build days were followed by four rework days.
dashboard.lesson: Execution quality could not compensate for an unsupported product form.

research.headline: The team learned more, but learned too late for the immediate decision.
details: The larger study confirmed the triage problem.
No working pilot existed for the investor demonstration.
The team lost the chance to compare behavior before and after a bounded change.
research.lesson: Additional research can be valid without being the highest-learning next step.

reject.headline: The dashboard was rejected, but the customer problem remained.
details: CSMs continued spending time across multiple systems.
The team failed to distinguish rejecting a proposed solution from rejecting the underlying job.
reject.lesson: A weak solution does not invalidate a supported problem.

learning_choices.text: Dashboards are bad and should be replaced by queues.
In Northline's eight-person pilot, exception-based triage improved speed and weekly use; evidence links were valuable; automatic next-action recommendations remain unproven.

learning_choices.quality: Too vague to guide future work
